title: Validating Against Real Standards
description: Checking AI-generated clinical records against HL7/FHIR conformance is not the same as checking whether the record is clinically correct — the gap this module trains you to close.

title: HL7 and FHIR in Practice
description: Read a FHIR resource and tell whether it says what the clinical record says — what HL7/FHIR standards actually guarantee versus what they don't, the four core resource types, chasing references to catch the ones that silently point at the wrong thing, reading a v2 message when that's what the system speaks, and the gap between a coded value being a legal member of its value set and being the correct one for this patient.

title: Structurally Complete, Clinically Wrong
description: Find the records that pass every automated validator and still misdescribe the patient — what a claims-edit engine actually checks versus what it can't, laterality and wrong-encounter mismatches, codes that contradict each other's own definitions, why diagnosis sequencing changes reimbursement even when every code is valid, and records that are internally consistent but describe a clinical timeline that doesn't actually happen.

title: Terminology Mapping and Its Traps
description: Judge whether a mapping between terminologies preserved the clinical meaning — why cross-terminology mapping is inherently lossy, one-to-many maps resolved by fallback defaults that ignore available context, granularity loss where a specific finding gets mapped to a general bucket, the local mapping tables no national standard watches over, and the source-first verification procedure that catches all three failure shapes.

title: HIPAA, Minimum Necessary and Real Privacy
description: Judge whether a record's handling meets privacy requirements in practice, not just on paper — identifying information hiding in free text beyond any labeled identifier field, minimum necessary as an actual purpose-scoping procedure with its narrow treatment exception, de-identification that satisfies Safe Harbor's checklist and still re-identifies through quasi-identifier combinations, what a Business Associate Agreement actually authorizes an AI vendor to do, and why an audit trail — not access control alone — is what catches inappropriate internal access.

title: Documentation Integrity and Compliance
description: Recognise coding patterns that create compliance exposure, whoever or whatever produced them — upcoding as a code-versus-documentation mismatch a pipeline can arrive at with no intent involved, unbundling and what modifier 59 actually has to prove, the MEAT standard for whether a chronic condition was genuinely addressed at this encounter, when documentation ambiguity calls for a non-leading clinician query instead of a guess, and building your own review's audit trail with the same rigor you've been applying to everything upstream of it.
